title: alloc failure: DLPack handoff + NVML breadcrumbs
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad to capture a weird OOM pattern seen when handing tensors across DLPack in the inference runtime. Includes commands I ran, small repro, error snippets, hypotheses, and next steps.

Context / symptoms:
- Intermittent CUDA OOM during inference pipeline that routes tensors between PyTorch and a C++ backend via DLPack (no obvious large allocation in user code).
- Happens on catkin-like steady traffic after a warm-up period (~30s) rather than immediately.
- Host: GPU A100-SXM with driver 535.113.01. Containers run with nvidia-container-toolkit 1.11.3.
- Affected node pool: dedicated-serving-3 (mixed spot/ondemand). Not seen on local dev machines.

Commands and outputs I ran (capture):
1) Basic health / driver:
$ nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY
==============
Attached GPUs : 1
GPU 00000000:00:1E.0
    FB Memory Usage
        Total : 40960 MiB
        Used  : 28641 MiB
        Free  : 12319 MiB

Note: used grows slowly during traffic. Not one giant jump.

2) Inside container: check libcuda linking
$ ls -l /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so*
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 19 Mar  5 09:12 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so -> libcuda.so.1
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 123456 Mar  5 09:12 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1

$ ldd /opt/runtime/lib/my_backend.so | grep cuda
    libcuda.so.1 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1 (0x00007f6d...)

3) Reproduce-ish run (localized micro-bench) to force DLPack handoff pattern (python snippet below). Observed: after ~2000 iterations, next allocation fails with CUDA out of memory.

python dlpack_repro.py:
----------------------
import torch
import numpy as np
from torch.utils.dlpack import to_dlpack, from_dlpack

# create many small tensors and send to C++ backend (simulated)
def run(n_iters=10000):
    t = torch.ones((1024,), device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
    for i in range(n_iters):
        a = torch.randn(1024, device='cuda')
        dl = to_dlpack(a)    # handoff to C++ (simulate by from_dlpack)
        b = from_dlpack(dl)  # back to PyTorch
        # do cheap ops to keep them alive for a moment
        c = b * t
        if i % 500 == 0:
            torch.cuda.synchronize()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run()
----------------------

Error snippet:
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 8.00 MiB (GPU 0; 40.00 GiB total capacity; 38.50 GiB already allocated; 7.50 MiB free; 35.00 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)

But nvidia-smi shows only ~1 GB growth at that time (fragmented).

4) NVML traces around the moment:
$ ./nvml-tools/nvml_trace --pid=12345 --interval=0.1 --duration=20
TIMESTAMP,PID,USED_MB,SM,ENG,DEC
...  13:22:01,12345,28510,0.04,0.02,0.00
...  13:22:25,12345,28640,0.05,0.03,0.00
...  13:22:33,12345,28648,0.05,0.03,0.00

Observation: used_MB increments in small steps (tens of MB at a time). Nothing shows a giant alloc that matches the error.

5) Kernel logs just after crash:
$ journalctl -u docker --since "13:22" | tail -n 60
[13:22:34] my_backend[23456]: Caught cudaError(2) at allocator.cpp:142 -- out of memory trying to allocate 8388608 bytes
[13:22:34] my_backend[23456]: Backtrace (most recent): ...
[13:22:34] my_backend[23456]: allocation patterns: small many allocations (~1-64KB) + occasional 8MB temp buffers

Repro notes:
- If I call torch.cuda.empty_cache() every 100 iterations, the failure is delayed but not eliminated.
- Setting CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 reduces nondeterminism but doesn't prevent eventual OOM.
- Forcing a single big allocation (torch.empty(10000000, device='cuda')) sometimes frees up a contiguous chunk and allows the next allocations to succeed (weird).

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Fragmentation in the CUDA device allocator + caching allocator behavior across DLPack boundary. DLPack/from_dlpack may create temporary tensors with different alignment/allocator metadata that confuses the caching/free patterns, leaving unusable holes.
2) Multiple runtimes linked into the process: PyTorch + custom C++ backend use different allocator default streams / contexts; buffer ownership semantics via DLPack might cause leak-like behavior where memory is held in another context unexpectedly.
3) Host libcuda mismatch or driver issue causing delayed accounting in NVML vs actual device free. (Lower probability given driver is recent, but still possible with certain container overlay combos.)
4) A bug in the custom backend's use of cuMemAlloc/cuMemFree when wrapping DLPack: double-free or free-after-async without stream synchronization leaving dangling allocations.
5) Interaction with MIG or host-level tooling (mps) causing per-process quotas to be hit subtly after many hides.

What I tried to mitigate / test (and results):
- Force single CUDA context for both PyTorch and backend: used cuInit+cuCtxAttach in C++ shim to attach to the existing context. Result: flakiness reduced but not eliminated.
- Build backend against the same CUDA runtime / cxxabi as the container's libtorch (matching tags): no change.
- Drop-in replace from_dlpack(to_dlpack(...)) with a memcpy path on host (GPU->CPU copy + CPU->GPU reupload) — completely avoided the OOM. Strong signal that the DLPack path is implicated.
- Run with PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:32 set to try to reduce fragmentation. Observed fewer failures but still happened after more iterations.
- Run glibc++ ABI check: ran strings /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6 | grep GLIBCXX_3.4.29 -- present.

Minimal repro idea:
- Script that repeatedly creates many small tensors with different allocation sizes and hands off via DLPack to a thin C++ process that just holds pointers for N iterations then releases. This should reproduce fragmentation if ownership semantics are wrong.

Potential instrumentation to add to runtime (next steps):
1) Add NVTX ranges around DLPack handoff + explicit cudaMemGetInfo() snapshots to detect discrepancies between allocator stats and NVML.
2) Enable PyTorch caching allocator debug stats at runtime: TORCH_CUDA_ALLOCATOR={"enabled":true, "stack_trace":true} (or equivalent env) to log freed vs reserved counts. (Investigate exact env flag for deployed libtorch version).
3) In C++ wrapper, before and after each DLPack import/export: call cuMemGetInfo, cuCtxGetApiVersion, and log stream ids + timestamps.
4) Temporarily switch DLPack path to CPU-copy path in canary to see reduction in incident rate (we already tested locally). If confirmed, proceed to keep fall-back for affected customers.
5) Add a small micro-benchmark that runs as part of nightly smoke to detect regressing fragmentation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is there any known historical bug with DLPack ownership semantics between libtorch 2.2 builds and our backend (C++ ABI mismatch)? Check GitHub PR history.
- Does running with NVIDIA driver's persistence mode ON change behavior? (Quick test planned).
- Can we get a core-dump of the allocator metadata (PTA/caching allocator) at the moment of OOM? Need to instrument or build debug-libs.
- Should we consider shimming DLPack to always copy for allocations under X bytes to avoid fragmentation? Tradeoff: performance cost vs reliability.

Quick checklist for next 48h:
- [ ] Add NVTX + cuMemGetInfo instrumentation to backend (Diego)
- [ ] Add metrics in Console: per-request memory deltas (Ruth)
- [ ] Run small fleet canary where DLPack path is replaced by CPU copy for 24h (Samir)
- [ ] Search GH for DLPack related fixes in libtorch 2.2 -> 2.3 (Samir)
- [ ] Try toggling NVIDIA persistence mode on one node and re-run repro (Ruth)

Useful references / links: 
- DLPack spec: https://github.com/dmlc/dlpack
- PyTorch DLPack docs: https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/dlpack.html
- NVML reference: https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/
- Related GH discussion: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/xxxxx (placeholder)

Notes to self:
- This one feels like fragmentation + cross-runtime ownership leak. The fact that CPU-copy eliminates it makes me suspicious of metadata around when buffer is freed.
- Keep an eye on reserved vs allocated numbers from the caching allocator; PyTorch reserved counts can be large but fragmentation causes shortage for contiguous allocations.

If anyone else picks this up: start from the minimal repro script + reproduce on a node, attach nvprof/nvtx, and then try both DLPack and CPU-copy modes back-to-back to compare memory curves.

End of scratchpad."
